Judgment required | After training and authorization, sort by label and material, wash, dry and press using approved processes, inspect, package and record; spills must be handled by trained personnel under the employer's emergency plan, without assuming untrained people will clean them up. Fit signals | Work activities for O*NET 51-6011.00 focus on controlling and operating equipment, processing information and inspecting quality. If you are willing to keep checking processes against labels and materials, can stand for long periods and perform repetitive movements, and will follow safety rules around chemicals and steam, these everyday demands may align more closely with your working style. Interest and personality tools serve only to design trials, not to judge hiring eligibility or performance.

Laundry and Dry-Cleaning Workers corresponds to U.S. 51-6011.00: operating or tending washing or dry-cleaning machines to clean industrial and household cloth items, suede, leather, fur, blankets, curtains, bedding and carpets, including stain removal and dyeing. Inspectable outputs | Records of sorted and inspected items, care-label and material assessments, stain treatment and process records, equipment programs and chemical use records, quality inspection and folding/packaging results, and explanations of exceptions and rewashing. Results must be traceable to labels, materials and process rationale.

Complete workflow | After training and authorization, verify item labels and materials → sort and treat stains using approved processes → operate washing and drying equipment according to instructions → press and inspect → verify order quantities and quality, package and record. Pause for unknown labels, spills or equipment faults and refer to the responsible person for verification; job duties are not operating instructions for beginners.

This job first checks: objects (garments and fabric items, care labels and fabrics, laundry solvents and detergents, washing and pressing equipment); inputs (item and order information, care labels and stain conditions, chemical and equipment instructions, safety and protection requirements); and deliverables (sorting and process records, equipment and chemical use records, quality inspection and packaging results, explanations of exceptions and rewashing). Treat anything unverified as pending verification; experience or intuition cannot replace label and material assessment.

Assess the work loop in four steps: verify inputs (confirm items, labels and materials) → define task boundaries (work within authorization and equipment capability, without independently treating unfamiliar fabrics) → execute and record (wash, dry and press according to procedures and retain records) → review and escalate (stop and report immediately if labels are doubtful, fabrics are damaged, chemicals spill or equipment malfunctions). A complete loop requires verifiable labels, materials and equipment programs, rather than merely checking whether an item looks clean.

Boundaries with adjacent roles | This page covers only the exact O*NET-SOC occupation 51-6011.00, Laundry and Dry-Cleaning Workers. Adjacent roles such as dishwashers, janitors and cleaners, maids and housekeeping cleaners, pressers and sewing machine operators differ in work objects, equipment types and responsibilities. Do not interchange them by job title alone or use proxy definitions in place of employer procedures, chemical safety requirements and equipment operating authorization.

paragraphs: Dishwashing direction | The core output is cleaned tableware and utensils returned to their places. This occupation handles fabric items and garments and involves material and stain assessment; different objects and processes mean the roles cannot be interchanged by title alone.

Comparison with janitors and cleaners | The main scope of 37-2011 is premises cleaning and waste handling, excluding housekeeping and domestic cleaning. This differs from laundry workers' garment washing and dry-cleaning equipment processes; verify responsibilities by code and work object.

Comparison with housekeeping and domestic cleaning | 37-2012 performs light cleaning in homes or commercial premises such as hotels and hospitals: making beds, replenishing linens, cleaning rooms and halls, and vacuuming, potentially including sorting and folding clothing. This occupation's specialized washing and dry-cleaning equipment processes have a different scope; a transfer is not automatic.

Comparison with pressers | 51-6021 presses and shapes items by hand or machine. Laundry workers also wash, dry-clean, remove stains and dye. Pressing tasks overlap, but overall scopes differ and do not automatically grant each other operating authorization.

Which interests, abilities and working styles matter more for laundry workers? This page discusses fit only through work samples and responsibility boundaries, without substituting personality labels for hiring eligibility or performance assessment.

Direct answer | Fit signals include willingness to keep checking processes against care labels and materials, ability to stand for long periods and perform repetitive movements, willingness to follow safety rules around chemicals and steam, and stopping equipment and reporting when labels are doubtful or equipment malfunctions. Personality labels are not the basis. Interest and personality tools can only help design trials, not judge hiring eligibility or performance.

Positive signals | You can sort and select processes by label and material; will complete training first and comply with approved processes and equipment permissions rather than devising formulas or parameters; and can identify fabric damage, color transfer or remaining stains and record rewashing.

Caution conditions | Risk signals include misreading care labels or materials, damaging fabrics through improper stain treatment, incorrect mixing or storage of solvents or detergents, missing protective equipment or inadequate ventilation, equipment overloading or incorrect programs, and color transfer from mixing items. If prolonged standing, repetitive movements or chemical contact are difficult to tolerate, weigh these as real costs.

Trial activity | An AC paper exercise, about 40 minutes, entirely fictional and involving no equipment or chemicals: order AC01 contains A1—A3, 3 items total, with simulated label text 'Plan Alpha only'; AC02 contains B1—B2, 2 items total, with simulated text 'Plan Beta only'; C1 is 1 separate item with its label missing. Alpha and Beta are fictional classification codes only, not washing, dry-cleaning or real care symbols. The delivery draft incorrectly states 'AC01 four items, AC02 two items, C1 assigned to Alpha, seven items total, all processed and ready for delivery.' Check item counts, grouping, pending verification and delivery status against the original cards, correct the draft and write an unsent inquiry. Do not select real processes, mixing ratios or temperatures from these codes.

Conclusion | Activity preferences align more closely with a combination of Realistic and Conventional interests (O*NET interest code RC, including physical and mechanical/electronic work). Interest codes can only help design trials, not judge hiring eligibility or performance.

Personality boundaries | This round did not establish predictive validity of personality scales for laundry-worker performance. Do not infer hiring decisions, ability or equipment permissions from labels; continue checking against AC feedback records.

Conclusion | RIASEC or personality frameworks can only help formulate questions. They cannot replace employer training, chemical and equipment safety requirements or evidence of actual work performance in this occupation. No tool conclusion constitutes a hiring, licensing or authorization judgment.

Chemical exposure and workplace fire risk | First check each chemical's SDS and the employer's risk assessment, verifying ventilation, containment and task protection. Petroleum-based solvents can be combustible or flammable; PERC is not flammable but poses health hazards, and other combustible materials may still be present. If a spill occurs, stop affected work, stay away from the exposure area and notify the responsible person. Trained, authorized personnel must handle it under the emergency plan; untrained people must not enter to clean it up. Smell alone cannot establish safety.

Machinery, steam and maintenance risks | Operate according to equipment instructions and training; do not open dry-cleaning machine doors or perform maintenance while running. Before cleaning or maintenance, authorized personnel must confirm shutdown, cooling and applicable energy isolation; pause if protective measures are abnormal. Pressing stop does not isolate all energy sources, including steam and electricity.

Unknown fabric labels and incorrect processing | First verify care labels, materials and approved processes. Stop and await verification for unknown labels or fabrics, referring them to the trained responsible person. O*NET lists spot testing as a duty; this does not authorize untrained people to test solvents or use flames independently. Do not perform chemical sample tests without permission; record damage and processing status.

Item counts, batches and delivery risks | Use orders, item IDs and batch identifiers to verify separation and quantities, and recheck processing and quality status before delivery. Matching counts do not establish acceptable quality; the six AC items are simulated records only.

Ergonomics and strain | Use the CCOHS hotel case to assess bending, twisting, reaching and handling. Improve workstations and carts, reduce repeated handling, and verify wheel maintenance and rest arrangements. Rotation among similar tasks does not guarantee risk elimination; do not apply the case's loads and staffing to all jobs.

These statistical descriptions are neither every employer's requirements nor promises of independent operation.

AC reference answer and four work samples: ① Count table: AC01=3, AC02=2, C1=1, total 6; the draft's 7 is 1 too many. ② Paper grouping: A1—A3 in Alpha, B1—B2 in Beta; C1 lacks a label and is listed separately pending verification, neither assigned to Alpha nor processed. ③ An unsent inquiry lists C1's original label, order association and authorized processing basis for the employer's responsible person to verify. ④ Revised delivery note: 'Six items total, classified on paper only; C1 pending verification. All actual washing and quality status is unverified; no processing or delivery has occurred.' Correct counts and categories do not prove clothing is clean or processing complete.

Seven-day plan, 20—30 minutes daily, on paper only: D1: copy orders and six item IDs; D2: verify 3+2+1=6 and the draft's excess of 1; D3: group Alpha/Beta by simulated text, leaving C1 pending verification; D4: read safety guidance and list no maintenance while running, with spills handled by trained personnel under the plan; D5: write the unsent inquiry and revise the delivery note; D6: ask a peer to check counts and unprocessed status, then revise; D7: assemble four work samples and verify the employer's equipment, chemicals, training, shifts and pay periods. The result is simulated work only; actual washing, dry-cleaning and pressing require separate training and authorization.

entries.answer: An AC paper exercise, about 40 minutes, entirely fictional and involving no equipment or chemicals: order AC01 contains A1—A3, 3 items total, with simulated label text 'Plan Alpha only'; AC02 contains B1—B2, 2 items total, with simulated text 'Plan Beta only'; C1 is 1 separate item with its label missing. Alpha and Beta are fictional classification codes only, not washing, dry-cleaning or real care symbols. The delivery draft incorrectly states 'AC01 four items, AC02 two items, C1 assigned to Alpha, seven items total, all processed and ready for delivery.' Check item counts, grouping, pending verification and delivery status against the original cards, correct the draft and write an unsent inquiry. Do not select real processes, mixing ratios or temperatures from these codes. AC reference answer and four work samples: ① Count table: AC01=3, AC02=2, C1=1, total 6; the draft's 7 is 1 too many. ② Paper grouping: A1—A3 in Alpha, B1—B2 in Beta; C1 lacks a label and is listed separately pending verification, neither assigned to Alpha nor processed. ③ An unsent inquiry lists C1's original label, order association and authorized processing basis for the employer's responsible person to verify. ④ Revised delivery note: 'Six items total, classified on paper only; C1 pending verification. All actual washing and quality status is unverified; no processing or delivery has occurred.' Correct counts and categories do not prove clothing is clean or processing complete. Seven-day plan, 20—30 minutes daily, on paper only: D1: copy orders and six item IDs; D2: verify 3+2+1=6 and the draft's excess of 1; D3: group Alpha/Beta by simulated text, leaving C1 pending verification; D4: read safety guidance and list no maintenance while running, with spills handled by trained personnel under the plan; D5: write the unsent inquiry and revise the delivery note; D6: ask a peer to check counts and unprocessed status, then revise; D7: assemble four work samples and verify the employer's equipment, chemicals, training, shifts and pay periods. The result is simulated work only; actual washing, dry-cleaning and pressing require separate training and authorization.

risks.consequence: Assess health hazards and workplace fire risk by specific substances and equipment; do not assert all solvents are flammable.
risks.mitigation: First check each chemical's SDS and the employer's risk assessment, verifying ventilation, containment and task protection. Petroleum-based solvents can be combustible or flammable; PERC is not flammable but poses health hazards, and other combustible materials may still be present. If a spill occurs, stop affected work, stay away from the exposure area and notify the responsible person. Trained, authorized personnel must handle it under the emergency plan; untrained people must not enter to clean it up. Smell alone cannot establish safety.
risks.scenario: Skin and respiratory exposure to solvents or detergents, inadequate ventilation or improper storage.

risks.consequence: May cause burns and pinch injuries.
risks.mitigation: Operate according to equipment instructions and training; do not open dry-cleaning machine doors or perform maintenance while running. Before cleaning or maintenance, authorized personnel must confirm shutdown, cooling and applicable energy isolation; pause if protective measures are abnormal. Pressing stop does not isolate all energy sources, including steam and electricity.
risks.scenario: Insufficient protection when operating or cleaning drums, presses, steam and drying equipment.

risks.consequence: May cause garment damage, compensation costs and reputational loss.
risks.mitigation: First verify care labels, materials and approved processes. Stop and await verification for unknown labels or fabrics, referring them to the trained responsible person. O*NET lists spot testing as a duty; this does not authorize untrained people to test solvents or use flames independently. Do not perform chemical sample tests without permission; record damage and processing status.
risks.scenario: Incorrect care-label or material assessment, stain treatment, temperature or program.

risks.consequence: May cause color transfer, incorrect delivery and complaints.
risks.mitigation: Use orders, item IDs and batch identifiers to verify separation and quantities, and recheck processing and quality status before delivery. Matching counts do not establish acceptable quality; the six AC items are simulated records only.
risks.scenario: Mixing storage or washing of items from different customers or processes.

risks.consequence: May cause lower-back and upper-limb strain.
risks.mitigation: Use the CCOHS hotel case to assess bending, twisting, reaching and handling. Improve workstations and carts, reduce repeated handling, and verify wheel maintenance and rest arrangements. Rotation among similar tasks does not guarantee risk elimination; do not apply the case's loads and staffing to all jobs.
risks.scenario: Prolonged standing, repetitive movements, bending and twisting.

risks.consequence: May cause injuries and compensation costs.
risks.mitigation: For spills or equipment faults, stop affected work, stay away from exposure and notify; trained, authorized personnel respond under the employer's emergency plan. Unknown labels await verification; do not independently perform reagent or flame tests.
risks.scenario: Continuing work despite chemical spills, equipment faults or unfamiliar fabrics.

salary.china_salary_note: Insufficient evidence: This round did not establish nationwide Chinese laundry-worker pay percentiles or starting pay strictly corresponding to U.S. 51-6011.00. The Hunan human resources authority's 2023 enterprise sample reports laundry-worker wage levels at the 10/25/50/75/90 percentiles of 2.81/3.19/3.40/3.93/5.02 ten-thousand yuan/year (published 2024-10-18). This is a provincial enterprise sample, neither nationwide figures nor 2026 quotations. The original page gives no sample size or pay components for this row; do not infer take-home or starting pay. For related resident services, repairs and other services, 2025 urban non-private and private annual average pretax pay is 70,226 and 52,059 yuan/year respectively, excluding individual businesses and freelancers. Keep the two types separate rather than combining them into a pay range; industry references do not replace occupational pay.
